children.title: Decision-Level Structure
children.top_down_role: Organization of assignments by branching depth and propagation context.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Level Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-level annotation of assignments in a CDCL search trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A CDCL trail is a sequence \(M=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m)\) of assigned literals partitioned by decision assignments. The decision level \(d(\ell_k)\) is the number of decision literals among \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k\). Thus level \(0\) contains assignments implied before any decision, a decision literal starts a new level, and every propagated literal receives the level current when its reason becomes unit. If \(D=\max_k d(\ell_k)\), then \(M\) decomposes uniquely into consecutive blocks \(M_0M_1\cdots M_D\), where each nonempty \(M_d\) for \(d>0\) begins with its level-\(d\) decision literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trail is partitioned into consecutive levels: root implications occupy level zero, each decision opens a new level, and subsequent propagations inherit that level.
assumptions_latex: The trail is consistent and assignments are appended chronologically.
Each nondecision assignment has a recorded unit-propagation reason.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=M_0M_1\cdots M_D\) with \(d(\ell)=d\) for every \(\ell\in M_d\).
review_flags: No directly relevant CDCL source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the Decision-Level Structure leaf and is internally coherent, but the record has no CDCL source with an inspectable locator. The stated convention for assigning propagated literals to levels therefore remains unsupported.

children.title: Implication Graph Structure
children.top_down_role: Dependency organization for propagated literals and conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Implication Graph Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed acyclic representation of decisions, propagations, and a conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a CDCL trail \(M\), its implication graph has one vertex for every assigned literal and, when a conflict exists, a distinguished vertex \( ot\). A decision vertex has no incoming reason edges. If literal \(v\) was propagated because the clause \((v\lor 
eg u_1\lor\cdots\lor
eg u_k)\) became unit, add edges \(u_j	o v\) for all \(j\). If a clause \((
eg u_1\lor\cdots\lor
eg u_k)\) is falsified, add \(u_j	o ot\). Every edge follows trail order, so the graph is acyclic, and every directed path to \( ot\) records a chain of assignments contributing to the conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices represent assigned literals and conflict; reason clauses create forward edges from antecedent assignments to their propagated consequence or to conflict.
assumptions_latex: Every propagated assignment has a clause reason recorded on the trail.
Edges are oriented from earlier antecedents to later consequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_M\) is a directed acyclic graph whose sink \(\bot\) represents the conflict.

notation.meaning: reason dependency from assignment u to consequence v

review_flags: No directly relevant CDCL source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the Implication Graph Structure leaf, and the edge orientation is consistent with acyclicity. No cited CDCL source supports the precise literal-vertex, reason-edge, and distinguished-conflict-sink conventions.

children.title: Level-Annotated Implication Paths
children.top_down_role: The correspondence between implication dependencies and decision levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Annotated Implication Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of decision levels along implication paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Annotate each assignment vertex \(v\) of the implication graph by its trail decision level \(d(v)\). For every reason edge \(u\to v\), the antecedent \(u\) occurs earlier on the trail than \(v\), and therefore \(d(u)\le d(v)\). Hence every directed assignment path \(v_0\to v_1\to\cdots\to v_k\) has nondecreasing level sequence \(d(v_0)\le d(v_1)\le\cdots\le d(v_k)\). A path may contain several vertices at the same level, but after it enters a higher level it cannot return to a lower one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision-level labels never decrease along a directed implication path because every antecedent precedes its consequence on the trail.
assumptions_latex: The graph edges arise from recorded unit-propagation reasons.
Decision levels are assigned from the chronological trail partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_0\to\cdots\to v_k\implies d(v_0)\le\cdots\le d(v_k)\).

notation.meaning: decision level annotating assignment vertex v

review_flags: No directly relevant CDCL source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the Level-Annotated Implication Paths leaf and follows the stated chronological convention, but neither that convention nor the resulting monotonicity claim has a cited CDCL source.

children.title: Conflict Analysis
children.top_down_role: Structural analysis of implication dependencies surrounding a conflict.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-UIP resolution analysis for a conflicting CDCL trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a conflicting trail at current level \(D>0\), its reason clauses, and the falsified conflict clause \(C\). Initialize \(L\leftarrow C\). While \(L\) contains more than one literal whose complement is assigned at level \(D\), choose the trail-latest such assigned literal \(v\), let \(R_v\) be its reason clause, and replace \(L\) by the resolvent of \(L\) and \(R_v\) on \(v\). Stop when exactly one literal of \(L\) is falsified at level \(D\). Output \(L\), its asserting literal, and backjump level \(b\), the maximum level of the other falsified literals, with \(b=0\) if none exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolve the conflict clause with reasons in reverse trail order until one current-level literal remains; output the asserting clause and its backjump level.
assumptions_latex: The current conflict occurs at decision level \(D>0\).
Every current-level propagated literal selected for resolution has a reason clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) is entailed by the clause database and contains exactly one literal falsified at level \(D\).

notation.meaning: reason clause for propagated literal v

review_flags: No directly relevant source for first-UIP conflict analysis was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithm is the correct role for this Conflict Analysis leaf, but no source supports the exact reverse-trail resolution procedure, stopping condition, asserting-literal convention, or backjump-level formula. These implementation-sensitive details require an authoritative CDCL citation.

children.title: Clause Learning
children.top_down_role: Production and retention of clauses derived from analyzed conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Clause Learning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution-derived learned clause as a checkable consequence of the current database.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the current clause database, and suppose conflict analysis produces a clause \(L	ext{ }\) through a finite sequence of resolution steps beginning with a clause of \(F\) and using recorded reason clauses from \(F\). The resolution sequence is a certificate that \(F\models L\). Adding the learned clause preserves the satisfying assignments: \[\operatorname{SAT}(F)=\operatorname{SAT}(F\land L).\] If \(L\) has exactly one literal falsified at the current level and all its other literals are falsified at levels at most \(b\), then after backjumping to \(b\), unit propagation makes that remaining literal true.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resolution derivation certifies that the learned clause follows from the database. Adding it preserves all models and can force an assertion after backjumping.
assumptions_latex: Every clause used in the resolution derivation belongs to or is entailed by \(F\).
The learned clause is not a tautology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\models L\) and \(\operatorname{SAT}(F)=\operatorname{SAT}(F\land L)\).
review_flags: No directly relevant source for CDCL clause learning was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolution derivation can serve as a certificate for entailment, and the model-preservation claim is plausible. However, no CDCL or proof-complexity source is cited, and the choice of certificate for the broader Clause Learning leaf should be confirmed against a source describing learning and assertion after backjumping.

children.title: Learned-Clause Quality
children.top_down_role: Structural characteristics affecting the usefulness of learned clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Clause Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Literal-block distance as a structural quality measure for a learned clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a learned clause at the instant of its creation, and let \(d(\neg\ell)\) be the decision level of the trail assignment falsifying literal \(\ell\in L\). The literal-block distance of \(L\) is \[\operatorname{LBD}(L)=\left|\left\{d(\neg\ell):\ell\in L\right\}\right|.\] Thus \(1\le\operatorname{LBD}(L)\le |L|\) for every nonempty learned clause. A smaller value means that the clause connects fewer decision-level blocks; using smaller LBD as higher quality is a database-management convention, not a logical-strength ordering between clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LBD counts the distinct decision levels represented among a learned clause's falsifying assignments. Smaller values are commonly treated as better retention signals.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is nonempty.
Every literal of \(L\) is falsified on the trail when the metric is computed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{LBD}(L)=|\{d(\neg\ell):\ell\in L\}|\) and \(1\le\operatorname{LBD}(L)\le|L|\).

notation.meaning: level of the assignment falsifying literal l

review_flags: No supplied source supports the precise LBD convention, including treatment of level zero.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Learned-Clause Quality leaf, but no source supports the precise LBD convention at clause creation, including whether decision level zero is counted. That convention materially affects the formula and bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonchronological Backtracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backjumping to the asserting level of a learned clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a learned asserting clause \(L\) with unique literal \(a\) whose complement is assigned at current level \(D\), compute \[b=\max\{d(\neg\ell):\ell\in L\setminus\{a\}\},\] taking \(b=0\) when the set is empty. Delete from the trail all assignments at levels greater than \(b\), retain assignments through level \(b\), insert \(L\) into the clause database, and run unit propagation. At the retained trail, every literal in \(L\setminus\{a\}\) is false, so \(L\) is unit and propagates \(a\). The jump is nonchronological whenever \(b<D-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Erase every trail level above the highest nonasserting level in the learned clause; the clause then becomes unit and forces its asserting literal.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is entailed by the current clause database.
Exactly one literal of \(L\) is falsified at the current decision level \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After backtracking to \(b\), unit propagation assigns the asserting literal \(a\).

notation.meaning: asserting literal of the learned clause

review_flags: No directly relevant source for CDCL backjumping was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the Nonchronological Backtracking leaf, but no cited CDCL source supports the backjump procedure. In addition, having exactly one current-level literal does not alone establish that every other clause literal remains false after backtracking to b; the asserting-clause trail conditions and treatment of literals unassigned by the jump need source-backed specification.

children.title: Clause Quality Metrics
children.top_down_role: Structural metrics used to characterize learned-clause usefulness.

knowledge_statements.title: Clause Quality Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multi-signal score representation for learned-clause retention decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a learned clause \(L\) at search time \(t\), a clause-quality record may be represented by \[q_t(L)=\bigl(\operatorname{LBD}_t(L),\ |L|,\ a_t(L),\ u_t(L)\bigr),\] where \(\operatorname{LBD}_t(L)\) is its literal-block distance, \(|L|\) its length, \(a_t(L)\) its activity, and \(u_t(L)\) its most recent use time. A retention policy is a specified ordering or score \(s_t(L)=\phi(q_t(L))\). The tuple itself is descriptive: no component logically implies another, and any claim that one clause is preferable requires the policy \(\phi\) to be fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clause retention can combine LBD, length, activity, and recency in a policy-defined score; the raw metric tuple does not itself impose an ordering.
assumptions_latex: All metric components are evaluated under a fixed solver convention.
The retention map \(\phi\) is deterministic once ties are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_t(L)=\phi(\operatorname{LBD}_t(L),|L|,a_t(L),u_t(L))\) defines the policy-specific clause ordering.

notation.meaning: quality-signal tuple for clause L at time t

review_flags: The metric tuple is architecture-dependent, and no solver-specific source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A multi-signal representation is compatible with the Clause Quality Metrics leaf, but the selected tuple and scoring map are solver-policy choices rather than a standard canonical definition. No solver-specific source supports these exact components or their interpretation.

children.title: Clause Activity
children.top_down_role: Dynamic relevance signals attached to clauses during search.

knowledge_statements.title: Clause Activity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict-driven bump-and-decay activity update for learned clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a decay parameter \(\rho\in(0,1)\). Initialize each learned-clause activity by \(a(L)=0\) and the bump increment by \(\Delta=1\). After each analyzed conflict, choose the clauses credited by the implementation and update \(a(L)\leftarrow a(L)+\Delta\) for each credited clause; then update \(\Delta\leftarrow\Delta/\rho\). Periodically multiply all activities and \(\Delta\) by the same positive constant to avoid overflow, which preserves their ordering. When other retention constraints are equal, larger \(a(L)\) indicates more recent or repeated conflict participation and gives the clause higher retention priority.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Credited clauses receive activity bumps while the bump scale grows geometrically, making older bumps relatively decay; common rescaling preserves the activity ordering.
assumptions_latex: Rescaling multiplies every clause activity and the current increment by the same positive factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update induces an exponentially recency-weighted ordering of credited conflict participation.
review_flags: No supplied source identifies the intended clause-activity update convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bump-and-decay algorithm fits the Clause Activity leaf, and common positive rescaling preserves ordering. Nevertheless, the credited-clause rule, increment update, retention interpretation, and claimed exponentially recency-weighted ordering are implementation-dependent and lack a cited source.

children.title: Clause Aging
children.top_down_role: Temporal decay and retention behavior for learned clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: Clause Aging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity-decay aging for learned clauses in a CDCL database.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each learned clause \(C\) have activity \(a_C\ge 0\), let \(0<\rho<1\), and let \(b_C(t)\ge 0\) be its relevance bump at event \(t\). Update \[a_C(t+1)=\rho a_C(t)+b_C(t).\] Equivalently, implementations may increase a global bump scale instead of explicitly multiplying every activity. At a reduction epoch, clauses with smaller activity are treated as older, subject to protection rules for locked, permanent, or otherwise retained clauses. Rescaling all activities by the same positive factor does not change their ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decay clause activities and bump recently useful clauses; lower activity identifies older deletion candidates, except clauses protected by retention rules.
assumptions_latex: Activity comparisons occur after logically equivalent global rescaling.
Protected clauses are excluded from age-based deletion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_C(t+1)=\rho a_C(t)+b_C(t)\), and smaller \(a_C\) represents greater age for retention ranking.

notation.meaning: activity of learned clause C at event t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation or inspectable locator supports the particular decay-and-bump aging convention, protected classes, or claimed implementation equivalence.

children.title: Quality-Sensitive Retention
children.top_down_role: Retention regimes combining clause quality with dynamic relevance.

knowledge_statements.title: Quality-Sensitive Retention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Learned-clause retention using structural quality and recent utility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a reduction epoch, let \(E\) be the learned clauses eligible for deletion. Assign each \(C\in E\) a quality tuple \(q(C)=(g_C,-a_C,|C|)\), where smaller glue or LBD value \(g_C\), larger activity \(a_C\), and shorter length are preferred. Order \(E\) lexicographically by increasing \(q\), retain a prescribed high-quality prefix, and delete only from the remaining suffix. Locked clauses and clauses in designated permanent classes are excluded from \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank eligible learned clauses by structural quality, activity, and size; retain the best-ranked clauses and delete only unprotected lower-ranked clauses.
assumptions_latex: Each eligible clause has defined quality, activity, and length values.
The deletion quota or retained-prefix size is fixed by the solver policy.
Locked and permanent clauses are ineligible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deletion is restricted to a suffix of \(E\) under the quality order induced by \(q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lexicographic tuple and prefix-retention procedure are solver-policy choices and have no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Clause Database Reduction
children.top_down_role: Removal regimes for controlling learned-clause database growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Clause Database Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic deletion of redundant learned clauses during CDCL search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a clause database \(D=O\cup L\), with original clauses \(O\) and learned clauses \(L\), construct an eligible set \(E\subseteq L\) by excluding locked, permanent, and policy-protected clauses. Rank \(E\) by the configured retention score and remove a quota \(R\subseteq E\) of lowest-priority clauses, deleting their watch-list entries consistently. Continue search with \(D'=D\setminus R\). Because every member of \(L\) was derived from \(O\), removing \(R\) preserves the models of \(O\), although it may weaken propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodically delete low-priority, unprotected learned clauses while preserving original clauses and consistent propagation data structures.
assumptions_latex: Every learned clause is logically implied by the original clause set.
No removed clause is currently required as a locked reason.
Watch and implication structures are updated consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D'=D\setminus R\) has the same satisfying assignments over the original variables as \(O\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction procedure, protection rules, and watch-list requirements are uncited. A relevant CDCL or solver-implementation source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Binary-Clause Specialization
children.top_down_role: Dedicated treatment of binary clauses within propagation and storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Clause Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implication-graph representation and separate handling of binary clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary clause \(C=(\ell_1\lor\ell_2)\) is represented by the two implications \[(\neg\ell_1\Rightarrow\ell_2)\quad\text{and}\quad(\neg\ell_2\Rightarrow\ell_1).\] Thus, whenever \(\ell_1\) becomes false, \(\ell_2\) is propagated, and symmetrically for \(\ell_2\). A specialized binary-clause store may retain these implication arcs separately from general watched clauses, provided insertion and deletion update both arcs atomically and conflict reasons remain recoverable as \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent each binary clause by two implication arcs, enabling direct propagation while maintaining a recoverable clause reason.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are Boolean literals.
The implication store updates both directions consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\ell_1\lor\ell_2)\equiv(\neg\ell_1\Rightarrow\ell_2)\land(\neg\ell_2\Rightarrow\ell_1)\).

notation.meaning: Boolean literals of the binary clause

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Boolean equivalence is standard, but the specialized storage, atomic update, and recoverable-reason claims require an authoritative implementation or SAT-solver source.

children.title: Binary-Clause Retention Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases governing preservation or removal of specialized binary clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Clause Retention Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safety boundaries for deleting specialized binary clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(\ell_1\lor\ell_2)\) be stored as two implication arcs. Deleting \(C\) is admissible only if it is learned or otherwise redundant, neither arc is needed to represent a nonredundant input constraint, and \(C\) is not the active reason for a trail assignment. Both arcs and all database references must be removed atomically. Removing only one arc breaks the symmetric representation; removing an active reason invalidates conflict analysis; removing a nonredundant original clause can enlarge the model set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary clause may be removed only when redundant and unlocked, with both implication arcs and references deleted atomically.
assumptions_latex: Binary clauses use the two-arc implication representation.
Conflict analysis expects every active reason to remain recoverable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Safe_\(\mathrm{delete}(C)\) requires redundancy, no active reason reference, and atomic removal of both implication arcs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deletion boundaries are implementation-dependent and uncited. In addition, conclusion_latex contains the malformed mixed expression `Safe_\(\mathrm{delete}(C)\)`; any sourced replacement should delimit the entire mathematical expression.

children.title: Literal Activity
children.top_down_role: Dynamic relevance scores associated with literals or variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Literal Activity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict-driven activity scores for selecting the next Boolean decision literal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an activity \(a(\ell)\ge 0\) for every literal \(\ell\). After conflict \(t\), add a nonnegative bump \(b_t(\ell)\) to literals selected by the conflict heuristic and apply decay \[a_{t+1}(\ell)=\rho a_t(\ell)+b_t(\ell),\qquad 0<\rho<1.\] At a decision point, choose an unassigned variable \(x\) maximizing a configured aggregate of \(a(x)\) and \(a(\neg x)\); phase selection then determines which literal of \(x\) is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bump literals implicated in conflicts, decay older activity, and branch on an unassigned variable with maximal aggregated literal activity.
assumptions_latex: The candidate set contains unassigned Boolean variables.
Ties are resolved by a fixed solver policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next decision variable lies in \(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\text{ unassigned}} A(x)\), where \(A\) aggregates the two literal activities.

notation.meaning: activity of literal ℓ after conflict t
variable score aggregated from its two literals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Literal-based activity, the aggregation into a variable score, and the decay convention vary across solvers; no source establishes this exact variant.

children.title: Phase Selection
children.top_down_role: Policies for choosing preferred Boolean assignment phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Phase Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of the truth value assigned to a chosen decision variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an unassigned decision variable \(x\), a saved phase \(s(x)\in\{0,1\}\), and an optional preferred phase \(p(x)\), choose the decision value by a fixed priority rule. Under phase saving, set \(v=s(x)\) when a saved phase exists; otherwise use \(v=p(x)\) when available, and finally a fixed default value. Enqueue the decision literal \(x\) if \(v=1\), or \(\neg x\) if \(v=0\), at a new decision level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After choosing a variable, select its value using saved phase, preferred phase, then a default, and enqueue the corresponding decision literal.
assumptions_latex: The selected variable \(x\) is currently unassigned.
The phase-priority rule is fixed for the current search regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The enqueued decision literal is \(x\) when \(v=1\) and \(\neg x\) when \(v=0\).

notation.meaning: most recently saved phase of x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The saved-phase, preferred-phase, and default priority order is a specific solver policy with no supporting citation.

children.title: Polarity Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, reversal, and diversification of assignment polarity preferences.

knowledge_statements.title: Polarity Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maintenance and revision of preferred Boolean phases across search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain for each Boolean variable \(x\) a preferred polarity \(p(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Whenever \(x\) receives an assignment that the configured phase-saving policy records, update \(p(x)\leftarrow x\)'s assigned value. Backtracking removes the trail assignment but does not erase \(p(x)\). A restart may preserve all preferred polarities, reset a designated subset, or replace them using an objective or solution hint. Subsequent phase selection consults the resulting \(p(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Record preferred variable values across backtracking, optionally reset or override them at restarts, and expose them to phase selection.
assumptions_latex: Each Boolean variable has a stored preferred polarity.
Updates follow a fixed phase-saving and restart policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Backtracking changes trail assignments but preserves \(p(x)\) unless an explicit reset or override applies.

notation.meaning: stored preferred Boolean value of variable x
Boolean variable whose polarity is managed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The persistence, restart reset, objective override, and solution-hint behavior are solver-specific and unsupported by a cited locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Policy Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified representation of common conflict-budget restart schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restart policy is represented by a positive budget sequence \((B_k)_{k\ge 1}\), where restart \(k\) occurs after \(B_k\) additional conflicts unless termination occurs first. Geometric policies use \(B_k=\lceil B_1r^{k-1}\rceil\) with \(r>1\). Universal policies use \(B_k=B_1u_k\), where \((u_k)\) is the Luby sequence. Adaptive policies define \(B_k\) from online statistics and restart when a specified predicate \(R_k\) becomes true. Restarting backtracks to the configured root level while retaining permitted learned state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restart families specify conflict budgets geometrically, universally, or adaptively, then backtrack while retaining policy-approved learned state.
assumptions_latex: Conflict counts are measured between successive restarts.
A restart preserves logical constraints and only resets designated search state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each policy determines a restart boundary through \(B_k\) or an adaptive predicate \(R_k\).

notation.meaning: k-th term of the Luby universal sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source defines the geometric, Luby, and adaptive families or the retained state. The record also presents policy families and operational rules rather than chiefly a representation; the proper kind should be reassessed after sourcing.

children.title: Cross-Engine Trail Coordination
children.top_down_role: Synchronization of Boolean assignments and integer-bound events.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Engine Trail Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-level trail discipline between Boolean and integer propagation engines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Boolean engine and an integer-bound engine share decision levels \(0,ots,d\). Every propagated Boolean literal or integer bound is appended with its decision level and a recoverable reason. Information exported by either engine is translated into an assertion accepted by the other engine without changing its level. On backtracking to level \(k\), both engines remove every trail entry with level greater than \(k\) and restore their reversible state to the corresponding synchronized markers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both engines attach levels and reasons to propagated facts, exchange assertions at the same level, and backtrack to synchronized trail markers.
assumptions_latex: Both engines use a common ordered set of decision levels.
Every exported propagation has a valid cross-engine explanation.
Each engine maintains a reversible marker at synchronized levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After backtracking to \(k\), both engine trails contain exactly their retained entries of level at most \(k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-engine protocol has no architecture source. The opening range `0,ots,d` is malformed and fails to define the shared decision-level set.

children.title: Cross-Engine Fixpoint Coordination
children.top_down_role: Propagation completion across SAT and integer engines.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Engine Fixpoint Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating SAT and integer propagation until a joint fixpoint or conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the current shared state and let \(P_B\) and \(P_I\) be sound, inflationary propagation operators for the Boolean and integer engines. Starting with \(S_0=S\), repeatedly apply enabled operators and import their consequences: \[S_{t+1}=P_I(P_B(S_t)).\] Stop with conflict if either operator derives inconsistency. Otherwise stop when \(S_{t+1}=S_t\), and return that jointly stable state. Under finite domains or another ascending-chain condition, this iteration terminates; fair scheduling is required when operators are applied incrementally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate sound Boolean and integer propagation, exchanging consequences until conflict or a state stable under both engines is reached.
assumptions_latex: \(P_B\) and \(P_I\) are sound and inflationary.
The state order satisfies an ascending-chain condition.
Incremental scheduling is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is either a conflict or \(S^*\) satisfying \(P_B(S^*)=P_I(S^*)=S^*\).

notation.meaning: shared propagation state after iteration t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this abstraction of CP-SAT coordination. Soundness and inflationarity plus an ascending-chain condition do not alone justify the stated common-fixpoint conclusion for the fixed composite iteration; suitable monotonicity, state-order, and scheduling hypotheses must be sourced and stated.

children.title: Wakeup Synchronization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Missed, duplicated, or delayed wakeups at engine interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Wakeup Synchronization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition ensuring no cross-engine propagator misses a relevant state change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each propagator \(p\), let \(W(p)\) be the set of Boolean assignments, integer-bound changes, and synchronization events on which \(p\) depends. A wakeup protocol is synchronization-safe exactly when every committed event \(e\in W(p)\) occurring after the last execution of \(p\) either enqueues \(p\) or is subsumed by a later queued event, and the joint-fixpoint test is permitted only when all cross-engine event queues are empty. Backtracking must cancel or reinterpret queued events whose supporting trail entries were removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relevant committed change must wake its dependent propagators, and joint stability may be declared only after all engine queues are empty.
assumptions_latex: Each propagator declares a complete dependency set \(W(p)\).
Event subsumption preserves every propagation consequence.
Backtracking identifies events supported by removed trail entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint quiescence is valid only if every cross-engine queue is empty and no unprocessed event belongs to any \(W(p)\).

notation.meaning: events capable of changing p's propagation result

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The wakeup and backtracking protocol is uncited. The claimed “exactly when” characterization is stronger than the stated assumptions establish and requires an authoritative architecture or propagation-scheduling source.

assumptions_latex: The Boolean trail \(T\) is consistent before the integer engine is invoked.
Every integer propagator returns either a valid implied literal with an explaining clause or a valid conflict clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every handed-off conflict is a clause entailed by the original model and falsified by the current trail, so CDCL analysis may consume it soundly.

notation.meaning: Current Boolean assignment trail shared by the engines.
Clause returned by the integer engine.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract handoff contract for a lazy-clause-generation-style CP-SAT architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a consistent Boolean trail \(T\) whose literals encode Boolean decisions and integer-domain facts. Run integer propagation to a fixpoint. If an integer propagator detects infeasibility under a finite reason set \(R\subseteq T\), it constructs the clause \(C=\bigvee_{r\in R}\neg r\). The handoff is admissible only if the original model entails \(C\) and every literal of \(C\) is false under \(T\). Insert \(C\) into the SAT clause database, invoke ordinary CDCL conflict analysis, backjump to the computed assertion level, and resume joint propagation. If no such conflict occurs, return the newly implied literals together with their explaining clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer engine hands CDCL only model-entailed clauses falsified by the current trail, after which ordinary conflict analysis and backjumping resume.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Handoff Between Engines

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the handoff container and states a plausible explanation-clause contract, but no inspectable source supports the CP-SAT handoff protocol, fixpoint sequence, or backjump integration.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Reason Resolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolution combines SAT reasons with clauses explaining integer propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a conflict clause \(C_0\) falsified by the current trail. While \(C_i\) contains more than one literal assigned false at the current decision level, choose a latest-assigned propagated literal \(p_i\in C_i\) and its explaining clause \(E_i\), where \(\neg p_i\in E_i\). Form \(C_{i+1}=\operatorname{Res}_{p_i}(C_i,E_i)=(C_i\setminus\{p_i\})\cup(E_i\setminus\{\neg p_i\})\), removing duplicate literals and discarding any tautological resolvent. Continue until the clause contains exactly one literal assigned false at the current decision level. Return that asserting clause and the largest decision level among its other literals as the backjump level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolve the conflict through SAT and integer explanation clauses on complementary pivot literals until an asserting learned clause and its backjump level are obtained.
assumptions_latex: Each propagated literal has a clause explanation entailed by the original model.
Every resolution step uses complementary occurrences of the same Boolean pivot in its two parent clauses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed-resolution derivation produces a model-entailed asserting clause and its corresponding backjump level.

notation.meaning: Reason clause containing the complement of pivot literal \(p_i\).
Pivot literal occurring in \(C_i\), whose complement occurs in \(E_i\).

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the permanent clause encoding of the current model.
\(A\) is a finite set of assumption literals applied only to the current solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns either a model of \(F\land\bigwedge_{a\in A}a\) or an assumption subset whose conjunction with \(F\) is unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard SAT solving under temporary assumptions, independent of a particular API.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F\) and an ordered assumption set \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), enqueue each \(a_i\) as a protected decision and propagate after every enqueue. Continue CDCL search while forbidding backtracking past assumptions that remain active. If a satisfying assignment is found, output its restriction as a model of \(F\land\bigwedge_{a\in A}a\). If conflict analysis reaches the assumption frontier, collect the assumptions whose decisions occur in the terminal conflict derivation and return a set \(U\subseteq A\) satisfying \(F\land\bigwedge_{u\in U}u\models\bot\). Remove all assumption decisions before the next solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temporarily assert assumptions, run CDCL, and return either a satisfying model or assumptions sufficient for the detected contradiction.
knowledge_statements.title: Assumption-Based Solving

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm matches assumption-based solving, but its protected-decision semantics, assumption frontier, core extraction, and cleanup behavior have no cited authoritative source.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a fixed constraint formula.
\(A\) is a finite set of admissible assumption literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\) is an infeasible assumption subset exactly when adding all assumptions in \(U\) makes \(F\) unsatisfiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an assumption core without requiring inclusion-minimality or minimum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a formula \(F\) and finite assumption set \(A\), a set \(U\subseteq A\) is an infeasible assumption subset, or assumption unsatisfiable core, when \[F\land\bigwedge_{u\in U}u\models\bot.\] Equivalently, no assignment satisfies both \(F\) and every literal in \(U\). The definition does not require minimality. It is inclusion-minimal precisely when every \(u\in U\) satisfies \[F\land\bigwedge_{v\in U\setminus\{u\}}v\not\models\bot.\] A minimum-cardinality core is an infeasible subset of least size among all subsets of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible assumption subset is any subset whose simultaneous assertion contradicts the base formula; minimality is an additional property.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Assumption Subsets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes an infeasible subset, an inclusion-minimal core, and a minimum-cardinality core, but no source is cited for the terminology or definitions.

children.title: Unsatisfiable-Core Minimization
children.top_down_role: Reduction of infeasible assumption subsets while preserving diagnostic utility.

assumptions_latex: \(U_0\) is a finite infeasible assumption subset for \(F\).
The solver can decide satisfiability of \(F\) under any tested subset of \(U_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(U\) is inclusion-minimal and infeasible, though it need not have minimum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-based extraction of an inclusion-minimal, not minimum-cardinality, assumption core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U\leftarrow U_0\). Visit each \(u\in U\) in a fixed order and solve \(F\) under assumptions \(U\setminus\{u\}\). If the result is unsatisfiable, replace \(U\leftarrow U\setminus\{u\}\); otherwise retain \(u\). Continue until every retained assumption has been tested against the current set, restarting affected tests when the implementation's ordering requires it. Output \(U\). The maintained invariant is \(F\land\bigwedge_{v\in U}v\models\bot\), and termination gives satisfiability of \(F\land\bigwedge_{v\in U\setminus\{u\}}v\) for each \(u\in U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly remove any assumption whose deletion leaves the formula unsatisfiable; the remaining core is inclusion-minimal, not necessarily smallest.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsatisfiable-Core Minimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deletion-based algorithm and its inclusion-minimal conclusion are mathematically coherent and fit the container, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

children.title: Incremental Core Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on core reuse across changing assumption contexts.

assumptions_latex: \(F_t\) and \(F_{t+1}\) are successive base formulas over a common assumption vocabulary.
\(U_t\) is an infeasible assumption subset for \(F_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Core reuse is sound only across revisions that preserve entailment of the old core contradiction; weakening or assumption remapping requires revalidation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between monotone model strengthening and revisions that invalidate prior cores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F_t\land\bigwedge_{u\in U_t}u\models\bot\). Reusing \(U_t\) at revision \(t+1\) is sound whenever \(F_{t+1}\models F_t\) and every literal in \(U_t\) retains its meaning, because then \(F_{t+1}\land\bigwedge_{u\in U_t}u\models\bot\). This guarantee ends if clauses supporting the contradiction are removed, integer encodings change without equivalence, or assumption literals are remapped. Concretely, with \(F_t=(\neg a)\), \(U_t=\{a\}\), and weakened \(F_{t+1}=\top\), the old core is no longer infeasible since \(F_{t+1}\land a\) is satisfiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old core survives model strengthening with stable assumption meanings, but weakening, re-encoding, or remapping can invalidate it.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Core Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strengthening condition and weakening counterexample correctly describe a core-reuse boundary, and failure_boundary is appropriate, but no source supports the incremental-engine claims.

children.title: Core Stability Across Revisions
children.top_down_role: Persistence of core relevance under incremental model or assumption changes.

assumptions_latex: All revisions use the same semantics for literals in \(A\).
The formulas are monotone strengthenings: \(F_{t+1}\models F_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every core valid at revision \(t\) remains infeasible at every later strengthening, although its minimality may be lost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistence of infeasibility, distinguished from persistence of core minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((F_t)_{t\geq 0}\) satisfy \(F_{t+1}\models F_t\), and let \(U_t\subseteq A\) obey \(F_t\land\bigwedge_{u\in U_t}u\models\bot\). Then for every \(s\geq t\), \[F_s\land\bigwedge_{u\in U_t}u\models\bot.\] Thus infeasibility of the old core is stable under monotone strengthening. Inclusion-minimality is not stable: a later revision may imply contradiction from a proper subset \(V\subsetneq U_t\). Stability also does not follow for nonmonotone revisions, even when the assumption vocabulary is syntactically unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under meaning-preserving model strengthening, old cores remain infeasible, but they may cease to be minimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Core Stability Across Revisions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The persistence of infeasibility under meaning-preserving monotone strengthening is precise, with minimality correctly excluded, but the property has no cited source.

children.title: Learned-Clause Validity
children.top_down_role: Validity requirements for clauses retained from conflict analysis.

assumptions_latex: \(F\) denotes the immutable semantic model, including valid Boolean encodings of integer constraints.
Every inference used to derive \(C\) preserves logical consequence from \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A learned clause is globally valid exactly when \(F\models C\); decision- or revision-dependent clauses require explicit guards or restricted lifetime.

notation.meaning: Semantic model encoded by the cooperating engines.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic validity criterion for clauses learned from SAT and integer reasoning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A learned clause \(C\) is globally valid for the cooperating solver precisely when \(F\models C\). If the derivation is valid only under temporary assumptions \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_k\}\), the reusable clause must be guarded as \[(\neg g_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg g_k\lor C),\] provided \(F\land\bigwedge_{i=1}^k g_i\models C\). A clause derived from search decisions alone is not globally retainable unless conflict analysis eliminates or guards those decisions. Likewise, a clause whose justification depends on a removable model component is valid only while that component remains active or appears among its guards.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A learned clause is reusable only if the persistent model entails it; temporary assumptions or removable constraints must be represented by guards.
knowledge_statements.title: Learned-Clause Validity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits learned-clause validity and gives a coherent guarded-clause criterion, but no source supports the cross-engine guarding and lifetime requirements.

children.title: Mixed-Resolution Validity
children.top_down_role: Validity requirements for resolution involving Boolean and integer reasons.

assumptions_latex: Each premise clause is entailed by the same persistent model \(F\).
Every nonpropositional inference is exported as a Boolean clause entailed by \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every resolvent produced by the mixed derivation is entailed by \(F\), including the final learned clause.

notation.meaning: Two clauses resolved on pivot p.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness invariant for resolution across SAT and integer explanation clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\models C_1\) and \(F\models C_2\), where \(p\in C_1\) and \(\neg p\in C_2\). Then \[F\models\operatorname{Res}_p(C_1,C_2)=(C_1\setminus\{p\})\cup(C_2\setminus\{\neg p\}).\] Consequently, a sequence mixing native SAT clauses with integer explanation clauses remains valid when every imported explanation is itself entailed by \(F\), all literals have a shared Boolean semantics, and each resolution step uses complementary occurrences of one pivot. If any imported reason is merely locally valid under unrecorded bounds or assumptions, this invariant does not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed resolution is sound when every SAT or integer premise is model-entailed and pivots have identical Boolean meaning across engines.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Resolution Validity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolution consequence invariant is mathematically correct and property is the proper content kind, but its application to mixed SAT–integer explanations lacks a citation.

children.title: Cross-Engine Resolution Boundary
children.top_down_role: Soundness limits at the interface between SAT clauses and external explanations.

assumptions_latex: The SAT and integer engines communicate through Boolean literals with fixed shared semantics.
A proposed external reason may depend on temporary contextual facts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Resolution may cross the engine boundary only through clauses entailed by the persistent model or clauses explicitly guarded by every temporary dependency.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface condition separating resolvable explanations from engine-local reasoning artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An engine-local inference may enter cross-engine resolution as clause \(C\) only if either \(F\models C\), or there is an explicit finite guard set \(G\) such that \[F\models\left(\bigwedge_{g\in G}g\right)\Rightarrow C,\] and the exported clause is \(C\lor\bigvee_{g\in G}\neg g\). Internal states such as unencoded arithmetic relaxations, stale bounds, heuristic deductions, or propagator caches cannot serve as resolution premises. Crossing this boundary without a model-entailed or fully guarded clause invalidates the learned-clause consequence invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only globally entailed or fully guarded clauses may cross from an integer engine into SAT resolution; private engine state is inadmissible.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Engine Resolution Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entailed-or-fully-guarded interface condition matches the terminal container, but the asserted exclusions for engine-local states require an authoritative architecture source.

assumptions_latex: Every deleted clause is redundant with respect to the permanent model or is a learned consequence of it.
No undeleted explanation, reason pointer, or certificate retains an operational dependency on the deleted clause.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting eligible learned clauses preserves the solution set and solver soundness, though it may reduce propagation strength.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic and operational conditions for safe learned-clause database reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq L\) be learned clauses satisfying \(F\models C\) for every \(C\in D\). Replacing \(F\land\bigwedge_{C\in L}C\) by \(F\land\bigwedge_{C\in L\setminus D}C\) preserves exactly the models of \(F\). Operational deletion is safe only when clauses currently locked as reasons, participating in an unfinished analysis, or referenced by external propagators are retained or their references are repaired. Permanent model clauses and clauses required to justify persistent cross-engine deductions are not eligible unless an equivalent persistent justification remains. Deletion can increase search but cannot create an incorrect model under these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entailed learned clauses may be deleted without changing solutions, provided no active reason, analysis, or external dependency still requires them.
knowledge_statements.title: Clause-Deletion Safety

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic deletion claim is coherent, and the operational qualifications are relevant, but reason locking, external references, and persistent-justification rules are implementation-sensitive and uncited.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsound External Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused by accepting an unjustified external implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(F=(x\lor y)\). The formula \(F\land
eg x\) is satisfiable, for example by \(x= ot\) and \(y=	op\). Suppose an external propagator nevertheless asserts \(p=x\) at the root and exports the unit clause \(C=(x)\), although \(F
ot\models x\). A subsequent solve under the temporary assumption \(
eg x\) encounters an immediate conflict between \(x\) and \(
eg x\) and can incorrectly report that the assumption is infeasible. The invalid unit clause also removes every valid model with \(x= ot\), so any learned consequence depending on it lacks a sound model-theoretic justification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unjustified root propagation of x can spuriously reject the satisfiable assumption not-x and exclude valid models with x false.
assumptions_latex: The solver accepts an external propagation without checking or recording a complete model-entailed explanation.
The propagated literal is not implied by the persistent model and the valid current context.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unjustified external propagation can exclude valid assignments and produce a spurious conflict or false infeasibility result under assumptions.

children.title: Relaxation Bound-Production Architecture
children.top_down_role: Covers CP-SAT's internal relaxation and bound-producing interfaces; general polyhedral theory and fixed-dimension algorithms remain in linked chapters.

Conforti, Cornuéjols, and Zambelli, Branch-and-Cut; Split and Gomory Inequalities; Structured Valid Inequalities

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Schrijver, Cutting Planes and Cutting Plane Proofs
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Balas, Lift-and-Project Cuts and Implementation Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Row Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-local generation of valid linear rows for a CP-SAT linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a discrete feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), a node domain \(D\), a relaxation \(P\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(F\cap D)\), and row generators \(\mathcal G\). For each \(g\in\mathcal G\), compute candidate inequalities \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) satisfying \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}z\leq\beta\) for every \(z\in F\cap D\). Add candidates whose violation at the current LP solution exceeds a prescribed tolerance, optionally after efficacy and redundancy filtering. Reoptimize and repeat until no accepted violated row remains or a resource limit is reached. Output the strengthened relaxation \(P'=P\cap\bigcap_{r\in R}r\), which still contains \(\operatorname{conv}(F\cap D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate valid inequalities violated by the current LP solution, filter and add them, then reoptimize until separation or resource limits stop the process.
assumptions_latex: \(F\cap D\neq\varnothing\).
Every generated row is valid for \(F\cap D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(F\cap D)\subseteq P'\subseteq P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic row-generation loop is mathematically coherent, but the node is specifically about CP-SAT architecture and no source supports its generation, filtering, scheduling, or stopping policy.

children.title: Incremental LP Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Lifecycle of relaxation rows, state, and repeated solves during search.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental LP Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-started maintenance of node LPs under bounds, rows, and objective updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an LP state \(S=(A,b,c,\ell,u,B)\), where \(B\) records a basis or equivalent solver state. When branching, propagation, or separation changes bounds or adds valid rows, update only the affected components to obtain \((A',b',c',\ell',u')\). If \(B\) is structurally compatible, use it as a warm start; otherwise construct a fresh state. Reoptimize until the updated LP is certified optimal, infeasible, or unbounded, and return its status, primal solution when available, and a validated dual bound. Warm-start information may affect running time but not the accepted status or bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Update changed LP bounds and rows in place, reuse a compatible solver state, and reoptimize while independently validating the resulting status and bound.
assumptions_latex: All inserted rows are valid for the current node domain.
The LP solver validates its reported terminal status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned status and dual bound refer to the updated LP \((A',b',c',\ell',u')\), not the preceding state.

notation.meaning: Reusable basis or equivalent LP state

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is plausible, but basis compatibility, in-place updates, terminal-status validation, and returned-bound behavior are solver-interface claims requiring an architecture or implementation source.

children.title: Dual-Bound Exchange
children.top_down_role: Transfer of relaxation-derived bounds into CP-SAT search.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Bound Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exchange of an LP dual certificate with an integer minimization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the node relaxation \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\geq b\}\) for the minimization objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). A vector \(y\geq0\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y=c\) certifies \(c^{\mathsf T}x\geq b^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in P\). If the node's discrete feasible set is contained in \(P\), the LP component may publish \(L=b^{\mathsf T}y\) as a search lower bound. When every feasible objective value is integral, the exchanged bound may be strengthened to \(\lceil L\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated dual-feasible LP solution supplies a lower bound to the discrete search; an integral objective permits rounding that bound upward.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\geq b\}\).
The discrete node-feasible set is contained in \(P\).
The search problem minimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x\geq L\) for every discrete node-feasible \(x\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x\geq\lceil L\rceil\) when all feasible objective values are integral.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

children.title: LP State Reuse Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting reuse of incremental relaxation state.

knowledge_statements.title: LP State Reuse Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary separating reusable warm-start data from reusable LP certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An LP state may be reused computationally only when its variable and row identifiers retain their meanings and the solver can reconcile all changed coefficients, bounds, rows, and objective terms. A previous basis may initialize reoptimization, but a previous primal solution, dual vector, status, or objective bound is not a certificate for the modified LP unless its feasibility and associated optimality conditions are revalidated. In particular, deleting rows, relaxing bounds, changing coefficients, or changing the objective can invalidate a formerly valid dual bound; incompatible structural changes require state reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse compatible bases as hints, but never reuse an old LP status or bound without validation after structural, bound, coefficient, or objective changes.
assumptions_latex: The maintained LP can change between search states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unvalidated certificates from the old LP cannot justify pruning in the modified search state.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between warm-start hints and reusable certificates is sound, but the asserted compatibility and reconstruction boundaries are implementation-dependent and uncited.

children.title: No-LP Regime
children.top_down_role: Solver operation without an active linear relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: No-LP Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Configuration regime in which the search does not solve linear relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A no-LP regime is a solver configuration in which no search node invokes an LP optimizer and no pruning decision uses an LP-derived primal or dual certificate. Feasibility propagation, conflict analysis, Boolean reasoning, domain reduction, incumbent bounds, and non-LP combinatorial bounds may remain active. Thus, for every node \(v\), the set \(R_v^{\mathrm{LP}}\) of solved LP relaxations is empty, while correctness still requires every pruning rule used at \(v\) to be independently valid for its discrete node domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver disables LP solves and LP-derived pruning while retaining propagation, conflict reasoning, incumbents, and other valid combinatorial bounds.
assumptions_latex: The underlying discrete search remains complete under its active branching and pruning rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_v^{\mathrm{LP}}=\varnothing\) for every search node \(v\).

notation.meaning: LP relaxations solved at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the regime container, but whether no-LP disables every node LP and every LP-derived certificate is a solver-specific configuration claim requiring documentation.

children.title: Default-LP Regime
children.top_down_role: Standard relaxation coverage and associated overhead profile.

knowledge_statements.title: Default-LP Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baseline solver-selected configuration of linearization, cuts, and LP effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A default-LP regime is a solver-defined configuration \(\theta_{m def}\) that constructs LP relaxations from the implementation's baseline set of eligible linearizations, invokes its baseline cut generators, and solves or updates those relaxations at nodes selected by its standard scheduling policy. If \(P_v(\theta_{m def})\) is the relaxation at node \(v\) with discrete feasible set \(F_v\), every admitted row must preserve \(\operatorname{conv}(F_v)\subseteq P_v(\theta_{m def})\). The word default identifies a configuration policy, not a mathematically canonical relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the solver's baseline choices for linearization, cuts, and LP scheduling; every admitted row must remain valid for the node's discrete feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The implementation specifies a baseline parameter vector \(\theta_{m def}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(F_v)\subseteq P_v(\theta_{m def})\) at every node \(v\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Default-LP is implementation-defined. A parameter or architecture source is required to establish which linearizations, cut generators, and scheduling policies constitute the default regime.

children.title: Max-LP Regime
children.top_down_role: Expanded relaxation coverage with greater bound-production effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-LP Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggressive solver configuration expanding eligible linearizations and LP strengthening effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A max-LP regime is a solver-defined configuration \(\theta_{m max}\) that enables the implementation's aggressive eligible linearizations, separation routines, and LP effort subject to compatibility and resource policies. For each node \(v\), its relaxation \(P_v(\theta_{m max})\) must contain \(\operatorname{conv}(F_v)\). The designation max refers to enabled implementation features; it does not assert that \(P_v(\theta_{m max})=\operatorname{conv}(F_v)\), that every valid inequality is generated, or that its bound is always strictly stronger than every other configuration's bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enable the implementation's aggressive LP features while preserving validity; “max” does not mean the integer hull or universal strict bound dominance.
assumptions_latex: The implementation specifies an aggressive parameter vector \(\theta_{m max}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(F_v)\subseteq P_v(\theta_{m max})\) for every node \(v\).

notation.meaning: Discrete feasible set at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The validity qualifications are careful, but the meaning of max-LP and the enabled aggressive features are implementation-dependent and unsupported by a source.

children.title: Integer-Rounding Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts produced through integrality-aware rounding of valid linear relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Rounding Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chvátal–Gomory rounding of an aggregated inequality for integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=x\in\mathbb R^n_+:Ax\leq b\u007d\), and let \(u\in\mathbb R^m_+\) satisfy \(u^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb Z^n\). Aggregating the rows gives \((u^{\mathsf T}A)x\leq u^{\mathsf T}b\) for every \(x\in P\). Because the left-hand side is integral whenever \(x\in\mathbb Z^n_+\), the rounded inequality \((u^{\mathsf T}A)x\leq\lfloor u^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor\) is valid for \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n_+\). It is an integer-rounding cut when it excludes a point of the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aggregate valid rows so the resulting coefficients are integral, then round down the right-hand side to obtain a valid cut for integer points.
assumptions_latex: \(u^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb Z^n\).
\(x\in\mathbb Z^n_+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u^{\mathsf T}A)x\leq\lfloor u^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor\) is valid for \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n_+\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Chvátal–Gomory rounding statement is mathematically standard and precise, but this nontrivial cut-family record has no cited evidence.

children.title: Gomory-Style Cuts
children.top_down_role: Tableau-inspired or equivalent integer-cut structures used by CP-SAT relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Gomory-Style Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-integer fractional cut derived from one simplex tableau row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a pure-integer tableau row has the form \(x_B=\bar b-\sum_{j\in N}\bar a_jx_j\), where \(x_B\in\mathbb Z\), every \(x_j\in\mathbb Z_+\), and \(f(t)=t-\lfloor t\rfloor\). If \(f(\bar b)>0\), then every integer solution satisfying the tableau row obeys the Gomory fractional inequality \(\sum_{j\in N}f(\bar a_j)x_j\geq f(\bar b)\). Consequently, this inequality removes the associated basic LP solution, at which all nonbasic variables are zero, while preserving every integer-feasible solution represented by the row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking fractional parts in a pure-integer tableau row gives an inequality that cuts off its fractional basic solution while preserving all integer solutions satisfying the row.
assumptions_latex: \(x_B\in\mathbb Z\) and \(x_j\in\mathbb Z_+\) for every \(j\in N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j\in N}f(\bar a_j)x_j\geq f(\bar b)\) is valid and excludes the associated basic fractional solution.

source_refs.locator: 9.4 Using Lift-and-Project to Choose the Best Mixed Integer Gomory Cut p. 117

source_witnesses.locator: 9.4 Using Lift-and-Project to Choose the Best Mixed Integer Gomory Cut p. 117

children.title: Rounding-to-Gomory Continuum
children.top_down_role: Structural overlap between general rounding cuts and Gomory-style variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding-to-Gomory Continuum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized scale-and-round family connecting elementary rounding with tableau-derived cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) be valid for \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n_+\), with \(a\geq0\). For every scale \(\lambda>0\), integrality and nonnegativity yield the valid scale-and-round inequality \(sum}_{i=1}^n\lfloor\lambda a_i\rfloor x_i\leq\lfloor\lambda b\rfloor\). Varying \(\lambda\) produces a family ranging from direct right-hand-side rounding when scaled coefficients are integral to nontrivial fractional-coefficient rounding. When the source inequality is an aggregated simplex tableau row, appropriate modular reformulation gives the corresponding Gomory-style member; the precise parameterization depends on the chosen rounding convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling a valid integer inequality before rounding creates a parameterized cut family; tableau-derived choices recover Gomory-style variants under an appropriate modular convention.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n_+\).
\(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) is valid for \(X\).
\(a\geq0\) and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(sum}_{i=1}^n\lfloor\lambda a_i\rfloor x_i\leq\lfloor\lambda b\rfloor\) is valid for every \(x\in X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scale-and-round inequality is valid under the stated nonnegativity assumptions, but its summation commands are malformed and the claimed continuum to a Gomory-style endpoint is convention-dependent and uncited. Source uncertainty therefore affects the defining representation.

children.title: Knapsack Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cut structures derived from bounded knapsack relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid inequalities separating the relaxation of a binary knapsack set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For weights \(a_i>0\) and capacity \(b\geq0\), define the binary knapsack set \(K=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i\leq b\}\). Given a continuous relaxation \(Q\supsetneq\operatorname{conv}(K)\), a knapsack cut relative to \(Q\) is a linear inequality \(\pi^{\mathsf T}x\leq\pi_0\) that is valid for every \(x\in K\) and violated by at least one point of \(Q\). Cover inequalities, lifted-cover inequalities, and other capacity-derived inequalities are members when they satisfy these validity and separation conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a chosen continuous relaxation, a knapsack cut is a capacity-derived linear inequality valid for every binary knapsack solution and violated by at least one relaxation point.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
\(Q\supsetneq\operatorname{conv}(K)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\subseteq\{x:\pi^{\mathsf T}x\leq\pi_0\}\), and some \(\bar x\in Q\) violates \(\pi^{\mathsf T}x\leq\pi_0\).

children.title: Cover Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cut structures derived from infeasible variable covers.

knowledge_statements.title: Cover Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical cover inequality for a binary knapsack constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n a_ix_i\leq b\}\), where \(a_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A subset \(C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a cover when \(\sum_{i\in C}a_i>b\). No feasible knapsack solution can select every item in \(C\); hence the cover inequality \(\sum_{i\in C}x_i\leq |C|-1\) is valid for \(K\). The cover is minimal when \(\sum_{j\in C\setminus\{i\}}a_j\leq b\) for every \(i\in C\), although minimality is not required for validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a set of items exceeds the knapsack capacity, at least one of them must be omitted, so at most one fewer than the cover size can be selected. Minimality is not required for this validity result.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i>0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
\(C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\sum_{i\in C}a_i>b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in C}x_i\leq |C|-1\) is valid for \(K\).

notation.meaning: A cover of the knapsack capacity

children.title: Flow-Cover Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cover-based cuts specialized to flow-capacity structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Cover Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-node capacitated fixed-charge flow set with binary activation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{(x,y):\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le b,\ 0\le x_i\le u_i y_i,\ y_i\in\{0,1\}\}\), where \(b,u_i>0\). If \(C\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in C}u_i>b\), define \(\lambda=\sum_{i\in C}u_i-b\) and \(r_i=(u_i-\lambda)^+\). The flow-cover inequality \[\sum_{i\in C}x_i-\sum_{i\in C}r_i y_i\le b-\sum_{i\in C}r_i\] is valid for every \((x,y)\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An over-capacity set of activated arcs yields a valid inequality coupling their flows with activation variables and residual capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(b>0\) and \(u_i>0\) for every \(i\).
\(C\) is a flow cover: \(\sum_{i\in C}u_i>b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in C}x_i-\sum_{i\in C}(u_i-\lambda)^+y_i\le b-\sum_{i\in C}(u_i-\lambda)^+\) is valid for \(X\).
review_flags: Exact flow-cover formulation lacks a directly matching supplied locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically plausible and fits the Flow-Cover Cuts leaf, but no cited source with an inspectable locator supports the exact inequality.

children.title: Clique Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts derived from mutual-exclusion structure among Boolean literals.

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict-graph clique inequality for binary literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be binary literals over variables \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), where each literal is either \(x_i\) or \(1-x_i\). Construct a conflict graph whose vertices are literals and whose edges join pairs that cannot simultaneously equal one in any feasible solution. For every clique \(Q\) of this graph, the clique cut \[\sum_{\ell\in Q}\ell(x)\le 1\] is valid for the feasible set and may strengthen its linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mutually conflicting binary literals forming a clique cannot have more than one true member.
assumptions_latex: Every edge of the conflict graph represents a valid pairwise incompatibility.
\(Q\) is a clique in that graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{\ell\in Q}\ell(x)\le 1\) is valid.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports conflict-graph clique cuts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique inequality is correctly stated for pairwise-incompatible binary literals and the property kind fits, but the record has no supporting citation.

children.title: Zero-Half Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts based on half-integral aggregation patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Half Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-half Chvátal–Gomory cut for a pure-integer linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(X=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax\le b\}\) with integral \(A\) and \(b\), choose \(u\in\{0,\tfrac12\}^m\) such that \(u^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb Z^n\). Aggregate the rows using \(u\), then round down the right-hand side to produce \[(u^{\mathsf T}A)x\le\lfloor u^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor.\] The inequality is a zero-half cut; separation selects a multiplier producing positive violation at the current relaxation point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half-multipliers aggregate integer rows; when the resulting left side is integral, rounding down the right side gives a valid cut.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\).
\(u\in\{0,\tfrac12\}^m\) and \(u^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb Z^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u^{\mathsf T}A)x\le\lfloor u^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor\) is valid for \(X\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports zero-half cuts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-half aggregation and rounding rule is mathematically standard and algorithm is an appropriate kind, but no source supports the exact construction or separation description.

children.title: Parity Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts exploiting odd-even structure in Boolean or integer relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forbidden-set description of one binary parity constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(p\in\{0,1\}\), and require \(\sum_{i\in S}x_i\equiv p\pmod 2\) for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). For every \(F\subseteq S\) with \(|F|\not\equiv p\pmod 2\), the forbidden-set parity cut is \[\sum_{i\in F}x_i-\sum_{i\in S\setminus F}x_i\le |F|-1.\] Together with \(0\le x_i\le1\), all such inequalities describe the convex hull of binary vectors satisfying this single parity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each subset having the forbidden parity generates an inequality excluding exactly that incompatible binary pattern; all such cuts describe the parity polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(\sum_{i\in S}x_i\equiv p\pmod 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forbidden-set inequalities and bounds describe \(\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\{0,1\}^S:\sum_{i\in S}x_i\equiv p\pmod 2\}\).

notation.meaning: subset having parity opposite to p

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the parity-polytope description.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forbidden-set inequalities and parity-polytope claim are precise, and representation fits the leaf, but the complete convex-hull assertion requires a cited source.

children.title: Disjunctive Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts derived from alternative feasible regions or branching disjunctions.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity criterion for a finite union of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\bigcup_{k=1}^q P_k\), where each \(P_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedron. A linear inequality \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is a disjunctive cut for a relaxation containing \(D\) precisely when it is valid for every disjunct: \[\sup_{x\in P_k}\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\qquad(k=1,\ldots,q).\] Consequently it is valid for \(D\) and for \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\); it cuts a relaxation point \(\bar x\) when \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}\bar x>\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear inequality valid on every branch of a finite disjunction is valid on their union and convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite union of polyhedra.
\(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is valid on every \(P_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is valid for \(D\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\).
